messages.author: 68dc38d7978d4aa0
messages.subject: Boas Coordinates
parts:
Dear all

I was wondering if it was possible to implement Boas Coordinates (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11692-020-09530-w) by somehow multiplying my Procrustes Coordinates in geomorph with the centroid size after GPA? Has anyone already used it?

Thank you in advance for your help!

Virus-free. www.avast.com

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Boas Coordinates
parts:
Here is how one can do that with one line of code:

boas <- simplify2array(lapply(1:length(Y.gpa$Csize), function(j) Y.gpa$coords[,,j] * Y.gpa$Csize[j]))

Keep in mind that this — as Fred Bookstein suggested to do — is not the same as a Procrustes superimposition without scaling configurations to unit size.  It is scaling, then superimposition, then unscaling.

Cheers!
Mike

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Boas Coordinates
parts:
Dear Basil,

The gpagen function does not have an option to omit scaling of configurations, a procedure that would not be a Procrustes alignment by definition.  Therefore, I would not call this “Procrustes superimposition without scaling”.  Klingenberg 2016 does not call this Procrustes superimposition but says it is a procedure analogous to Procrustes superimposition.

I would also like to note that Klingenberg introduced this approach toward the end of this paper without really exploring its limitations, for which I think there could be many.  I do not wish to posit that GPA has no limitations but it is more difficult to imagine a configuration where the solution that minimizes the sum squared differences between corresponding landmarks of configurations does not also tend to find smaller distances between those landmarks compared to distances between non-corresponding landmarks, between configurations.  Without the scaling to unit size, there would be many cases — especially if size varied substantially — that this would not be the case.  In other words, not scaling configurations sort of removes the homologous nature of landmarks, mathematically.  Boas coordinates do not do this, and I believe Bookstein and colleagues are keenly aware of this.  Note the sequence of papers.  In my opinion, Boas coordinates are a better solution (application) for finding a “conformation space” than what Klingenberg was proposing as a concept.  Consider it an improvement, a refinement of the concept.

There might be functions out there that do not need to include scaling as a portion of a Procrustes superimposition but I would argue that doing this might only be valid in the few cases where size variation is small, so small that it does not remove the homology of corresponding points.  But if this were true, then doing this type of Superimposition (cannot emphasize enough that it is not Procrustes superimposition!) or calculating Boas coordinates would likely converge on solutions.

Finally, let’s not forget about sliding semilandmarks.  Klingeberg (2016) does not consider these cases.  I cannot believe that a sliding semilandmark algorithm would work in this alternate superimposition.  Boas coordinates offer no obstacle to using semilandmarks, however there is a caveat to what the original scale should be, as it would be calculated before sliding the landmarks, yet the sliding of landmarks happens after configurations have been rendered the same in size.  Jim Rohlf recently discussed this on Morphmet.  I personally see this as a digitization problem, where an assumption of approximate uniformity in landmark position might be implied (lest one wishes to have poor outcomes from the sliding algorithm…).  But it is also my opinion that the proper sliding of landmarks is a large research void that is yet to be fully explored.  That is a discussion for another day!

Cheers!
Mike

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Boas Coordinates
parts:
Hi Basil,

The function, plotAllometry, can do this for you.  Look at the example in the help file for inspiration.  When you get to the part that looks like this:

pc.plot <- plotAllometry(fit, size = gdf$Csize, logsz = TRUE,...

the object, pc.plot, has scores (pc,plot$PC.points) which are the form space variables.  Note that we cite Mitteroecker et al. (2004) for the method, and I believe Klingenberg also cites this or other work by those authors, so subtle differences in what is meant by “form space” could exist.

Best,
Mike
